title: BOAZ WANTED TO REDEEM RUTH—BUT ANOTHER MAN HAD THE LEGAL RIGHT BEFORE HIM
paragraphs: BOAZ WANTED TO REDEEM RUTH—BUT ANOTHER MAN HAD THE LEGAL RIGHT BEFORE HIM

He Had the Heart to Love Her, the Means to Redeem Her, and the Desire to Give Her a Future. But One Man Stood Between Ruth and Her Redemption. What Happened Next Reveals Something Breathtaking About the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Ruth 3:12–13 | When Love Refuses to Take Shortcuts, Redemption Becomes Even More Beautiful
Imagine finally meeting someone who sees beyond your broken past.

Someone who doesn't treat your scars like a warning sign. Someone who knows you've suffered, knows you've lost, knows you have nothing impressive to offer—and still considers you worthy of kindness, dignity, and a future.
Now imagine discovering that this person genuinely wants to make you part of his family.
But there's a problem.
Someone else has the first legal opportunity.
And the man who wants to redeem you refuses to violate what is right, even if doing the right thing means he might lose you.
That was the tension hanging over Ruth's future on a dark threshing floor in Bethlehem.
And buried inside that ancient moment is a truth many Christians desperately need to recover.
Not every closed door means God has abandoned you. Sometimes the person who truly loves you will refuse to open a door dishonestly—even when walking through it would give them everything they want.
But there is something even deeper here.
Because Ruth's story is not merely about finding a good husband.

It is about a vulnerable widow, a faithful man, an unresolved legal obligation, and the astonishing way God was quietly preparing a family line through which the Savior of the world would eventually come.
And if you've ever wondered whether God can still write something beautiful after your life has fallen apart, stay with this story.
The ending is far greater than a wedding.
Before Ruth ever stood on that threshing floor, she had already stood beside graves.
She was a Moabite widow.
Her husband had died. Her father-in-law had died. Her brother-in-law had died. Naomi, her mother-in-law, had also lost her husband and both sons.
Three women had been left widowed, and eventually only Ruth and Naomi continued together toward Bethlehem.
There were no promises of financial security. No guaranteed new marriage. No assurance that the people of Bethlehem would welcome a foreign widow.
Ruth could have returned to Moab and sought another future.
Naomi had even encouraged her to do so.
But Ruth made a declaration that still echoes through Scripture:
“Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.”
—Ruth 1:16, KJV
Those words were more than affection for Naomi.
They expressed Ruth's decision to identify herself with Naomi's people and with the God of Israel.
And notice something extraordinary.
Ruth did not know that Boaz was waiting in Bethlehem.
She did not leave Moab because she had received a marriage proposal.
She chose faithfulness without knowing how the story would end.
Some of the most important acts of obedience in your life will happen before you have any idea what God intends to do with them.
You may be caring for someone who cannot repay you.
You may be starting again after a devastating loss.
You may be remaining faithful to Christ while everyone around you seems to be moving forward faster.
You may be doing the right thing and wondering why it has not made your life easier.
Ruth knew something about that kind of uncertainty.
She arrived in Bethlehem not as a celebrated woman with influential connections, but as a widow who needed food.
And so she went into the fields to glean.

In ancient Israel, God's law made provision for the poor, the foreigner, the widow, and the fatherless by requiring landowners to leave portions of the harvest available for them (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 24:19–22).
Ruth was not simply wandering through someone's private property hoping nobody would notice.
She was seeking provision through a practice rooted in God's concern for vulnerable people.
Then Scripture says something beautifully understated.
Her path brought her into a field belonging to Boaz.
Ruth 2:3 describes her arrival in a way that, from the human perspective, sounds almost accidental.
She happened upon his field.
But readers who know the ending can see God's providence unfolding through ordinary circumstances.
Not every act of providence arrives with thunder.
Sometimes it looks like a hungry widow entering a field.
Sometimes it looks like an ordinary workday.
Sometimes it looks like one person deciding to treat another person with unusual kindness.
Boaz noticed Ruth.
But what he noticed was not merely her appearance.
He had heard how she cared for Naomi after her husband's death.
He knew she had left her father, mother, and homeland to live among a people previously unfamiliar to her.
And he spoke words that revealed his understanding of her faith.
“The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.”
—Ruth 2:12, KJV
Under whose wings thou art come to trust.
Remember those words.
Because the image of sheltering wings returns at the very moment Ruth asks Boaz to become her redeemer.
And that connection changes the way we understand the story.
As the harvest continued, Naomi recognized that Boaz was one of their family redeemers.
The Hebrew term is גֹּאֵל (gōʾēl), commonly transliterated go'el.
It refers to a kinsman or family redeemer, someone who could act to protect or restore important family interests under Israel's covenant laws and customs.
Depending on the situation, redemption could involve recovering family property, helping a relative in distress, or fulfilling other kinship obligations.
But we need to be careful here.

The Book of Ruth brings together family land redemption and the preservation of a deceased man's family name. It resembles aspects of levirate marriage, described in Deuteronomy 25:5–10, but that law specifically addresses a deceased man's brother.
Boaz was not identified as Ruth's deceased husband's brother.
The narrative describes a broader family-redeemer situation, and we should not pretend that every legal detail is fully explained.
That distinction matters.
Because faithful Bible interpretation does not require us to invent details that Scripture has not given.
The beauty of this story is already powerful enough.
Naomi devised a plan for Ruth to approach Boaz at the threshing floor after he had finished eating and drinking and had lain down.
Ruth followed her instructions.
In the darkness, Boaz awoke and discovered a woman lying at his feet.
He asked who she was.
Her answer was courageous.
“I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.”
—Ruth 3:9, KJV
The word translated “skirt” in the King James Version comes from the Hebrew כָּנָף (kānāf).
It can refer to a wing or the edge of a garment.
Here, Ruth's request to spread his garment over her is widely understood as an appeal for marital protection and commitment.
Do you see the beautiful connection?
Earlier, Boaz had prayed that Ruth would find refuge beneath the wings of the God of Israel.
Now Ruth was asking Boaz to extend that protective care to her through his role as a family redeemer.
The man who had spoken about God's shelter was being invited to become an instrument of that shelter.
This is not a license to claim that every Christian is guaranteed a Boaz or a marriage.
It is a picture of faithful human action within God's providential care.
And what Boaz said next reveals his character.
He blessed Ruth.
He praised her loyalty.
He assured her that he would do what she requested.
But then came the sentence that changed everything.
“And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I.”
—Ruth 3:12, KJV
Read that again.
“There is a kinsman nearer than I.”
Boaz wanted to help Ruth.
He was willing to act as her redeemer.
But another relative had a prior claim.
And Boaz would not simply ignore him.
Can you imagine what Ruth might have felt when she heard those words?
Scripture does not record her private emotions in that moment, so we should not pretend to know them.
But the uncertainty was real.
She had approached Boaz with a serious request.
He had responded favorably.
Yet the outcome remained unresolved.
Then Boaz continued:

“Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, that if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, well; let him do the kinsman's part: but if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, then will I do the part of a kinsman to thee, as the LORD liveth: lie down until the morning.”
—Ruth 3:13, KJV
There it is.
The integrity of Boaz.
He did not promise Ruth an outcome he had no right to guarantee.
He did not pretend that his personal desires canceled another man's prior opportunity.
He did not manipulate the situation by concealing what he knew.
He acknowledged the nearer redeemer and committed himself to resolving the matter properly.
Boaz was willing to redeem Ruth, but he was not willing to obtain her future through dishonesty.
And that is where this story confronts us.
Because we live in a world where people frequently use desire to justify disobedience.
“I love this person, so the circumstances don't matter.”
“I need this opportunity, so I have to bend the truth.”
“God knows my heart, so surely He understands why I crossed that boundary.”
But wanting something deeply does not automatically make every method of obtaining it righteous.
Boaz teaches us something our impatient hearts often resist.
A good desire does not give us permission to pursue it through wrongdoing.
That truth applies far beyond marriage.
It applies to business decisions.
Financial desperation.
Romantic relationships.
Ministry opportunities.
Personal ambitions.
Promises made when nobody is watching.
The question is not only whether you want something good.
The question is whether you are willing to honor God while pursuing it.
And sometimes that means accepting the possibility that obedience may cost you what you wanted.
Think about Boaz.
He could not know with certainty how the nearer redeemer would respond.
The other man might accept the responsibility.
Boaz's opportunity to marry Ruth might disappear.
Yet he chose the honorable path.
That is what makes his conduct so compelling.
His integrity was not dependent on knowing that everything would work out in his favor.
He acted rightly before the outcome was settled.
Somebody reading this is standing in a similar place right now.
You know what you want.
You have prayed about it.
You have imagined the future.
You can almost see what life would look like if everything finally fell into place.
But there is a boundary you cannot cross without compromising your obedience to Christ.
And the temptation is whispering that perhaps this one exception would be understandable.
Listen carefully.
God's grace is not permission to manipulate, deceive, betray, or take what is not yours.
Grace forgives sinners who come to Christ in repentance.
Grace also teaches believers to renounce ungodliness and live uprightly (Titus 2:11–12).
The same Savior who welcomes the repentant calls His people to follow Him.
And following Him may require refusing a shortcut.
Even when the shortcut looks like the answer to your prayers.
Now return to Bethlehem.
Morning came.
Boaz did not leave the matter unresolved.
Ruth 4 tells us that he went to the city gate, where public legal and community matters could be handled before witnesses.
He found the nearer redeemer and gathered ten elders of the city.
Then he presented the matter concerning Naomi's family land.
At first, the nearer redeemer expressed willingness to redeem it.
But when Boaz explained the obligation involving Ruth and the preservation of the deceased man's name in connection with the inheritance, the man withdrew.
His concern was that the arrangement might endanger his own inheritance.
Scripture does not provide every detail behind that concern.
It does, however, record his decision.
He would not proceed.
Boaz then publicly declared his intention to acquire the family property and take Ruth as his wife, preserving the deceased man's name in connection with his inheritance.
The elders and people witnessed the transaction.
And the man who had refused to violate the proper process was now free to act.
There is something quietly magnificent about that.
Boaz did not need to become dishonest to secure his future with Ruth.
He did not need to make the nearer redeemer look evil.
He did not need to undermine the public process.
He brought the matter into the light.
And in the light, the way forward became clear.
That does not mean every faithful person will receive the outcome they desire.
Scripture never promises that obedience guarantees marriage, financial prosperity, or the restoration of every earthly dream.
Sometimes obedience leads through suffering.
Sometimes the door remains closed.
Sometimes faithfulness is costly for reasons we do not understand.
But the worth of obedience does not depend on whether it produces the result we hoped for.
God is worthy of obedience because He is God.
And Boaz's story reminds us that righteousness matters even when the future is uncertain.
Then the narrative reaches its beautiful resolution.
“So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife.”
—Ruth 4:13, KJV
The foreign widow who had entered Bethlehem grieving and vulnerable became part of a household with a future.
But the story did not end with the wedding.
The LORD gave Ruth conception, and she bore a son.
The women of Bethlehem celebrated with Naomi.
The child was named Obed.
And then the writer revealed why this family story mattered far beyond its immediate circumstances.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And generations later, the Gospel of Matthew would include Ruth and Boaz in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:5–6 identifies Boaz and Ruth as ancestors in the line leading to David, and Matthew 1:16 brings that genealogy to Jesus, who is called Christ.
Consider what that means.
A grieving Moabite widow became part of the family history through which the promised Messiah would enter the world.
Not because Ruth possessed extraordinary social status.
Not because her life had been free from tragedy.
Not because she had somehow earned God's mercy through flawless performance.
The narrative shows God's providence working through suffering, loyalty, kindness, lawful action, and ordinary human faithfulness.
A woman who once faced an uncertain future became part of a story that would eventually point the world toward its Redeemer.
And here we arrive at the deepest truth.
Boaz was a redeemer within Ruth's story. Jesus Christ is the Redeemer to whom the whole biblical story ultimately leads.
We must understand that distinction.
Boaz was a real man acting within Israel's family and inheritance customs.
Jesus did not become our Savior by reenacting every legal step at Bethlehem's city gate.
The New Testament presents His redemption on an infinitely greater scale.
Boaz could address a family's earthly vulnerability.
Jesus addresses humanity's bondage to sin and the need for reconciliation with God.
Boaz could take Ruth as his wife.
Jesus gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
Boaz acted at personal cost within the responsibilities of his community.
Jesus gave His own life as the sacrifice for sinners.
The connection is a meaningful biblical foreshadowing, not an assertion that every detail in Ruth is a direct prophecy about Christ.
And the contrast is glorious.
The Greek New Testament uses the language of redemption to explain what Jesus accomplished.
In Ephesians 1:7, Paul writes:
En hō echomen tēn apolytrōsin dia tou haimatos autou, tēn aphesin tōn paraptōmatōn.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.”
—Ephesians 1:7, KJV
The Greek word ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis) means redemption or release through the payment of a ransom.
Paul connects our redemption directly to Christ's blood and the forgiveness of our trespasses.
Not to our religious achievements.
Not to our donations.
Not to our social standing.
Not to our ability to erase our own past.
To the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is the center of the Gospel.
And it matters enormously because there is a difference between needing a second chance in life and needing salvation from sin.
Ruth needed provision, security, and the restoration of family interests.
Every human being, whether wealthy or poor, married or single, admired or forgotten, needs reconciliation with a holy God.
Scripture says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
Our greatest problem is not simply that life has wounded us.
It is that sin has separated us from the God who created us.
And no amount of self-improvement can pay the debt of sin.
No public reputation can make us righteous.
No charitable contribution can purchase forgiveness.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
His resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
His mercy is real.
And His invitation is not reserved for people whose lives look respectable.
Listen to what Peter wrote:
“Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold... But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.”
—1 Peter 1:18–19, KJV
Not silver.
Not gold.
Not anything you could place in an offering envelope.
The precious blood of Christ.
Perhaps you came into this article thinking about Ruth and Boaz, but somewhere along the way you started thinking about yourself.
About the mistakes you still remember.
The relationships you damaged.
The sins you concealed.
The people you disappointed.
The years you cannot recover.
Maybe you have learned how to smile in church while carrying shame that nobody sees.
Maybe you know all the right worship songs but struggle to believe that God could still welcome you after what you have done.
Maybe your life has become a carefully maintained appearance of spiritual strength while your private world is falling apart.
And perhaps the hardest question you have ever asked is one you have never spoken aloud.
Can Jesus really forgive someone like me?
The Gospel answers that question by pointing not to your worthiness, but to Christ's sufficiency.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we convinced everyone we had changed.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve another chance.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes His grace astonishing.
And genuine grace does not leave us comfortable in rebellion.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because our wrongdoing was exposed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
Faith is not simply admiring Jesus as a good example.
It is trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
And the Christian life is not a performance designed to earn God's love.
It is a life increasingly transformed by the grace already given in Christ.
Perhaps you need to hear that today.
Your past is real.
Your sins matter.
The consequences of your choices may not disappear overnight.
Some broken relationships may require difficult conversations, accountability, restitution, and patient rebuilding.
But your past does not possess authority greater than the risen Christ.
If you belong to Jesus, shame is not your savior, and condemnation is not your identity.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1, KJV
Do not mistake that promise for permission to continue knowingly in sin.
It is the assurance that those united to Christ are no longer under the condemnation their sins deserve.
And that is why repentance and hope belong together.
You can confess the truth without surrendering to despair.
You can acknowledge your wrongdoing without believing that redemption is impossible.
You can stop hiding because the Savior already knows the worst about humanity and still gave Himself to save sinners.
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Some people are waiting for a Boaz when what they most desperately need is to surrender to Jesus.
They are hoping another human being will finally make them feel valuable.
They are waiting for a relationship to repair an identity that has been shattered by rejection.
They are asking another imperfect person to carry the weight that only the Savior can bear.
But no husband can become your Messiah.
No wife can become your salvation.
No romantic relationship can cleanse your conscience before God.
And no earthly love can replace the eternal love revealed at Calvary.
Boaz was a blessing to Ruth.
He was not her god.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And if marriage never comes, if the relationship ends, if the answer to your prayer looks different from what you imagined, the Gospel remains true.
You are not spiritually incomplete because you are unmarried.
You are not beyond God's care because your story has included loss.
And you are not disqualified from serving Christ because your life does not resemble someone else's testimony.
Your ultimate hope is not that God will send you a Boaz.
Your ultimate hope is that God has sent His Son.
And His name is Jesus.
There is another part of this story we must not overlook.
Boaz acted with integrity when he could have acted selfishly.
Ruth acted courageously while remaining vulnerable.
Naomi, despite her earlier bitterness, witnessed God's kindness unfold in ways she could not have predicted.
And the nearer redeemer, whose name is not given in the narrative, made a decision that allowed Boaz to proceed.
Different people.
Different responsibilities.
Different choices.
Yet the sovereign God was working through the ordinary realities of their lives.
This should humble us.
We cannot see the whole story while we are living inside one chapter.
We often want God to explain the ending before we obey Him in the present.
We want certainty before faithfulness.
Results before sacrifice.
Vindication before patience.
But Ruth's story invites us to trust the Lord without pretending we can predict every outcome.
God's providence is not an excuse for passivity.
Ruth gleaned.
Naomi advised.
Boaz acted.
The elders witnessed.
Human responsibility and divine providence were not enemies in this narrative.
And they are not enemies in the Christian life.
Pray.
Tell the truth.
Work faithfully.
Honor your commitments.
Repent when you sin.
Seek wise counsel.
Protect those who are vulnerable.
Do not use spiritual language to excuse manipulation.
And when the future remains uncertain, remember that God is not confused simply because you are.
The Lord knows what you do not know.
He sees what you cannot see.
And even when His providence is difficult to understand, His character remains trustworthy.
That is why this story deserves more than a passing reaction on social media.
It deserves reflection.
Perhaps it has exposed a shortcut you were about to take.
Perhaps it has reminded you of someone you treated carelessly.
Perhaps it has confronted the belief that your past makes you unworthy of ever being loved again.
Or perhaps you have realized that you have been seeking from people what only Christ can give.
If that is you, don't hide behind another polished religious comment.
Be honest before God.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes an honest confession becomes the beginning of a conversation that another struggling believer desperately needs to have.
There is no shame in asking fellow believers to carry your burdens in prayer.
And if you have experienced Christ's mercy after a season of failure, consider sharing a little of your testimony.
Someone reading may believe their own story is beyond redemption.
Your words might help them look toward the Savior who has not stopped calling sinners to repentance and faith.
That is also why I want to ask something more of you.
Not merely to react to this article.
Not merely to finish reading and move on.
Help carry the truth of Jesus Christ beyond the people who already know where to find it.
Not for my recognition.
Not to make a post appear successful.
But because someone among your friends may be silently wrestling with grief, guilt, spiritual confusion, or the belief that God could never receive them.
You may never know who reads it at two in the morning.
You may never know which sentence causes someone to open their Bible again.
You may never know which struggling believer needed to remember that Christ's grace is greater than the shame they have been carrying.
Not because these words have power apart from God's Word, but because the biblical truths behind them deserve to be revisited.
Return to Ruth chapters 1–4.
Read the entire account.
Then read Matthew 1, Ephesians 1, Romans 3–5, and 1 Peter 1.
Let Scripture—not merely an emotional moment—shape what you believe about redemption.
There is also a deeper way to walk with us.
These resources exist to help people study the Bible, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, and continue learning beyond a single social media article.
It is a practical way to help sustain and expand the work of creating Scripture-centered articles, discipleship resources, and Christian teaching.
Some believers may choose to include that support within their planned giving.
But I want to make something absolutely clear.
The New Testament teaches that Christian generosity should come from a willing heart, not pressure or compulsion.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
It can become one practical expression of your desire to help more people encounter biblical truth.
These are expressions of appreciation, not the purpose of discipleship.
The greater invitation is to help build a community that keeps returning to the Scriptures, encouraging one another, and pointing people to Jesus Christ.
Pray for the work.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage another believer.
Help someone understand the Bible.
Support your local church faithfully.
And keep growing in Christ.
It is about making Jesus known.
And that brings us back to Ruth.
Back to Bethlehem.
Back to the darkness of the threshing floor.
Back to a widow who had no certainty about what morning would bring.
Boaz told her that another man had the prior opportunity to redeem.
He would not ignore that responsibility.
He would not take what was not yet his to claim.
He would act honorably, even with an uncertain outcome.
Then, when the nearer redeemer declined, Boaz stepped forward openly and fulfilled his commitment.
Ruth became his wife.
Their son became an ancestor of David.
And through David's line, the promised Christ came into the world.
What began with graves in Moab became part of the genealogy of the Savior.
What began with hunger in a field became part of a story that still speaks of God's providence.
What began with a vulnerable widow seeking protection became a testimony to the Lord's kindness working through faithful people.
But even that beautiful ending is not the greatest redemption in Scripture.
The greatest redemption happened when Jesus Christ gave Himself for sinners and rose victorious over death.
And this is the question I want to leave with you.
Have you admired the beauty of redemption while refusing to come to the Redeemer?
Have you been hoping for your circumstances to change while resisting the Savior who calls you to repent?
Have you been trying to earn through religious activity what Christ offers through grace?
You do not need to purchase His mercy.
You cannot.
You do not need to make your past disappear before coming to Him.
You cannot.
Come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
Confess your sin.
Trust His finished work.
Follow Him as Lord.
And let His Word reshape the way you live.
If you already belong to Christ, remember this when obedience becomes difficult: you are not called to manufacture a beautiful ending through compromise.
You are called to be faithful to the Savior who has redeemed you.
Because the heart of this story is not that every Ruth eventually finds a Boaz.
It is that God's redemptive purposes are greater than the chapters we can see.
And the heart of the Gospel is not that every earthly tragedy receives a happy ending in this lifetime.
It is that Jesus Christ died and rose again so that sinners who trust in Him may receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and everlasting life.
Ruth did not know what morning would bring—but generations later, the world would learn that her story had become part of the road to Bethlehem's greatest gift: Jesus Christ.
